title: Trent’s meritorious cause is Christ’s passion—same as our imputation
source_text: XXXII. Idem vero Concilium, Sess. 6. cap. 7. docet istius justificationis quae juxta ipsum non est sola peccatorum remissio, sed & sanctificatio, & renovatio interioris hominis, per quam homo fit ex injusto justus, & ex inimico amicus, ut sit haeres secundum spem vitae aeternae, causam meritoriam esse Dominum nostrum Jesum Christum, qui sua sanctissima passione in ligno crucis, nobis justificationem meruit, & pro nobis Deo Patri satisfecit; ac neminem posse esse justum, nisi cui merita passionis Domini nostri Jesu Christi communicantur. Quod certe reipsa idem est cum eo quod Theologi nostri significare intendunt; quando dicunt justitiam Christi nobis imputari, & nos per illam coram Deo justificari. Quid enim, ut jam saepius inculcatum, dum sic loquuntur, aliud sibi volunt quam remissionem peccatorum nostrorum, & adoptionem in Dei filios, & regni coelestis haeredes, nullis nostris meritis deberi: sed soli Christi merito & satisfactioni, quae nobis a Deo vere donantur & communicantur?
pass_a_gloss: The same Council, Sess. 6, ch. 7, teaches that of that justification which according to it is not remission of sins alone but also sanctification and renovation of the inner man, by which a man becomes just from unjust and a friend from an enemy, so that he may be an heir according to the hope of eternal life, the meritorious cause is our Lord Jesus Christ, who by his most holy passion on the wood of the cross merited justification for us and satisfied God the Father for us; and that no one can be just unless the merits of our Lord Jesus Christ’s passion are communicated to him. Which is certainly in reality the same as what our theologians mean when they say that Christ’s righteousness is imputed to us and that we are justified before God by it. For what else, as has already often been inculcated, do they intend when they so speak than that the remission of our sins and adoption as God’s children and heirs of the heavenly kingdom are owed to none of our merits, but to Christ’s merit and satisfaction alone, which are truly given and communicated to us by God?
pass_b_english: Trent: meritorious cause is Christ’s cross-passion communicated—else none is just.
That is what Reformed mean by imputing Christ’s righteousness: free remission and adoption by his alone-communicated merit.
